title: Emphasis (em)
description: The em element for stress emphasis that changes meaning, with a full em vs i comparison.
subject: html
html:
The <em> tag adds stress emphasis — emphasis that can genuinely change what a sentence means when read aloud, not just italic styling.

Syntax

<em>stressed text</em>

Basic Example

<p>I <em>never</em> said she took the money.</p>

Browser output: the word "never" renders in italics. But notice what it does to meaning: stressing a different word in that same sentence — "I never said she took the money" — implies someone else did.

How It Works

The browser applies font-style: italic by default, identical to <i>. The difference lives entirely in meaning: <em> tells a machine "reading this word with stress changes the sentence's meaning," which <i> never claims.

Important Attributes

AttributePurpose
— none —Only universal global attributes apply

Real-World Example

<p>Do <em>not</em> refresh the page while your file is uploading.</p>

Emphasizing "not" is exactly the kind of instruction where stress genuinely matters — skimming past it changes the instruction's meaning entirely.

Comparison: i vs em (quick recap)

<i> marks an alternate voice or category of text (technical terms, titles, foreign words) with no implied stress. <em> marks genuine stress emphasis that can change meaning. Full comparison table: Italic Text.

Common Mistakes

  • Using <em> purely because italics look nice, with no real stress or meaning change intended — that belongs in <i>
  • Overusing <em> across a whole paragraph, which flattens its impact until nothing reads as genuinely emphasized

Best Practices

  • Use <em> sparingly — reserve it for words that truly change a sentence's meaning if stressed
  • Per spec, nested <em> (emphasis inside emphasis) increases the degree of stress — rarely used, but good to know it exists

Accessibility Considerations

Screen readers can change intonation when reading <em> content, though the exact behavior varies by screen reader and voice engine — it's a real, if inconsistent, functional signal.

SEO Considerations

Same as <strong> — treat any ranking benefit as unconfirmed and minor at best.

Browser & Modern HTML Notes

Valid and stable in HTML5, with meaning unchanged from earlier HTML versions — unlike <b> and <i>, <em> and <strong> were always defined semantically, never purely presentationally.

Mini Practice

  1. Write the same sentence three times, emphasizing a different word each time with <em>, and explain how the meaning shifts.
  2. Find a sentence online misusing <em> purely for italic styling, and explain why <i> would be more correct.
